newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel suggests German tax cuts could begin in '98.
newsitem.headline: Waigel suggests German tax cuts could begin in '98.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Wednesday suggested for the first time that the Bonn government would be willing to bring forward part of its planned income tax cuts by one year to 1998.

Speaking to members of his Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) party at its annual Ash Wednesday gathering, Waigel said he could imagine cutting the entry-level tax rate and dropping the top rate to below 50 percent from 53 percent now.
"A condition, however, is that a part of the financing measures proposed by the tax reform commission also take effect in 1998," Waigel said.

The government coalition, made up of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), the CSU and the liberal Free Democrats (FDP), has proposed a 30 billion mark net tax cut in 1999 that would cut the top rate to 39 percent.

The opposition Social Democratis (SPD), which can block parts of the tax reform with its majority in the upper house of parliament, has urged Bonn to bring forward the tax cuts to 1998. It opposes government plans to partly finance the reform by raising value added taxes.
Oskar Lafontaine, the feisty SPD party boss, repeated his strong objections to the government's tax proposals in an interview with the daily Sueddeutsche Zeitung.
Lafontaine has said repeatedly that while the government's tax reform would relieve low-wage earners and the wealthy, the large masses of the middle class would benefit less.

He told the newspaper that the tax reform should instead begin with an entry-level income tax rate of 19 percent and leave the top rate at 53 percent. He could also imagine cutting the entry rate to 15 percent from today's 26 percent.

Lafontaine repeated his opposition to raising value added taxes and offered to meet the leaders of Kohl's coalition in an effort to iron out differences over the tax plan and avoid holding the bill up in parliament's mediation committee.

"On the basis of goodwill we do not need more than a week," he said. "We would not need the mediation committee because everyone who needs to decide is in the SPD leadership, the CDU leadership or in the coalition."
A senior Kohl aide said the government would present its tax reform bill at the end of April and talks with the SPD could then begin immediately.
Lafontaine dismissed demands from Waigel and other government officials that the SPD play a constructive role by presenting its own alternatives instead of just criticising.

"In light of current developments in the 1997 budget, which are frightening, I call on Mr Waigel to say clearly how large a fall in tax revenues he thinks the 1998 budget can stand. Then the SPD will quickly present its own offer," he said.
